abstract: The lung is constantly exposed to environmental challenges, so its immune status must be tightly regulated. Alveolar macrophages (AMs) are myeloid cells that play a key role in maintaining lung homeostasis and preventing excessive inflammatory responses. Here, we report that AMs rely on the protein kinase p38a to regulate the major histocompatibility complex class II (MHCII) expression, identifying one way in which AMs may contribute to allergic and malignant lung disease. Using genetically modified mice in which p38a is specifically deleted in myeloid cells, we show that p38a controls the antigen presentation capacity of AMs. Mechanistic studies indicate that p38a downregulates MHCII expression in AMs by restraining the expression of the transcriptional activator CIITA, which involves the p38a-regulated protein kinase MK2 and histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6). We found that mice with p38a deleted in myeloid cells have an enhanced adaptive immune activation, which results in increased response to allergic airway inflammation but reduced tumor growth in the lung. Our results reveal that p38a signaling is required to maintain the levels of immunosuppression that preserve lung homeostasis, and show how dysregulation of this pathway may contribute to inflammatory lung diseases.
